The bans have been introduced ahead of the bushfire season because many parts of eastern Tasmania are already dry and warmer weather is expected. The bans apply to reserved land within; Break O'Day, Brighton, Central Highlands, Clarence, Derwent Valley, Dorset, Flinders, George Town, Glamorgan-Spring Bay (including Maria Island), Glenorchy, Hobart, Huon Valley, Kingborough,(including Bruny Island), Latrobe, Launceston, Northern Midlands, Sorell, Southern Midlands, Tasman, and West Tamar. Waters from the Southern Ocean collide with the towering sea cliffs of the Tasman Peninsula, creating spectacular rock formations, including caves and arches. The coastal vegetation grows precariously close to the edges of the cliffs, creating a blanket of green that contrasts with the surging surf below. Australia’s highest sea cliffs have walkers on the award-winning, multi-day Three Capes Track in awe. Day walkers can also discover a slice of this beauty high atop the cliffs on shorter coastal walks at Cape Hauy , Cape Raoul and the world-famous big wave mecca, Shipsterns Bluff. Easily visited from Hobart, Tasman National Park is an area of great beauty and natural diversity that can be explored by car, from the water, on foot and even by helicopter. Get your parks pass Page Content ​​​​​​In the State’s far south-east, linked to the rest of the island by a short bridge over a dredged canal, lie the Tasman and Forestier peninsulas. The Tasman National Park protects the eastern and southern coastal regions of both, which are joined by a narrow isthmus at Eaglehawk Neck. Undoubtedly, the Park’s greatest heroes are its sea cliffs – Australia’s highest. Striking dolerite spires rise from the Tasman Sea, culminating in capes Hauy, Pillar, and Raoul. All three capes can be explored from well-graded tracks, including on the renowned multi-day Three Capes Track , or via one of the 60 Great Short Walks to Cape Raoul or Cape Hauy . For a different perspective, experience the spectacular scale of the cliffs from below by tour boat or kayak – or for hard-core surfers, from the barrel of a giant wave off Shipstern Bluff – one of the most dangerous surf locations in the world. These waters are also a divers’ mecca, with enormous sea caves, shipwrecks, and abundant, diverse and unique marine life. The varied coastline (sheltered to stormy), the proximity to the continental shelf, and a meeting of ocean currents, combine to create a habitat for ... everything, really. Whatever marine experience you choose, whether it be fishing, surfing, cruising, snorkelling or diving, expect to be accompanied by seals , dolphins – and, in season, whales . For an easier view of other internationally acclaimed geological marvels, the sea has sculpted from softer sandstones and mudstones, the wondrous Tasmans Arch, Devils Kitchen, Blowhole ​and Remarkable Cave – all these sights just a few steps from your vehicle. But perhaps the Park’s best-kept secret is its plant life. From towering eucalypt forests to colourful coastal heathlands, there’s a landscape you’re sure to enjoy. And with such diversity comes​ a great variety of Tasmania’s familiar birds and animals providing endless hours of pleasure. If lazing on a beach or camping with family and friends is more your style, Fortescue Bay (the end point for the Three Capes Track ​), is one of Tasmania’s most beautiful campsites, set amongst tall blue gums and stringybarks, with a golden arc of wide sand. Here you can take your pick of peninsula pleasures: Swimming, snorkelling, scuba diving, surfing, kayaking, boating, fishing, rock climbing and walking ... It’s no wonder Tasman Peninsula is lauded as a nature-lovers’ playground. ​ Nature and conservation Show more/less ​​​Internationally acclaimed geological marvels abound within Tasman National Park, with the greatest heroes the soaring dolerite sea cliffs guarding the Park's eastern and southern boundaries. These cliffs end defiantly in the majestic capes of Pillar, Hauy and Raoul. Elsewhere, less resistant sandstones and mudstones are sculpted into extraordinary features such as Tasmans Arch, The Blowhole, and Remarkable Cave. The Park's varied coastline and offshore islands provide abundant habitats for marine life . Australian fur seals, little penguins , whales , dolphins and a plethora of fish and marine invertebrates flourish in the rich waters, fed by the upwelling of nutrients provided by the meeting of ocean currents and proximity to the continental shelf. On offshore islands, and around the capes, seals haul out and seabirds nest. For such a tiny corner of the State, it's an impressive fact that over one third of Tasmania's plant species grow in this geographically isolated area, including more than sixty threatened species. Eucalypt forests, heathlands, moorlands, cliffs, beaches and offshore islands provide a diversity of habitats for an equally rich and diverse wildlife . Birdlife is abundant, with several threatened species finding sanctuary, including the swift parrot, hooded plover, wedge-tailed eagle and white-bellied sea eagle. And the usual suite of Tasmanian mammals (wallabies, wombats, quolls, bettongs, potoroos, antechinus, bandicoots, and possums) is now in company with an ever-increasing healthy population of Tasma​nian d​evils. Learn more about the conservation efforts of our devils on the Save ​the Tasmanian Devil Program website . For more information on our wildlife please see Tasmania's wildlife . Visit our caring for wildlife page for more information on interacting with and protecting our native animals. ​ Cultural heritage Show more/less The Tasman Peninsula is within the homelands of the Pydairerme clan of the Oyster Bay nation. These people favoured the coastal bays to camp, where they feasted on the ocean's bounty. They also travelled to inland areas of the peninsulas and carried out a variety of social, cultural, economic and spiritual activities. The Tasman Peninsula contains a number of significant sites, mainly in the form of middens, quarries and artefact scatters. The Park and adjacent reserves are considered an area of high cultural significance because of the diversity of Aboriginal sites present. These sites and the greater landscape have a strong and continuing connection to the Tasmanian Aboriginal community. The early 1800s saw the arrival of whalers and sealers, who'd come to exploit the abundant marine mammals ​ for their oil. Shortly after, by 1830, this industry was shut down, for the Tasman Peninsula was set to become a prison for hundreds of convicts transported from Britain. The peninsula's peculiar geography and geology guaranteed it the perfect choice: isolated by a narrow isthmus and foreboding sea cliffs, sheltered bays for anchoring, rich with tall timbers for shipbuilding, and soft sandstones for shaping into a settlement. By the turn of the twentieth century, convict transportation ceased, and the peninsulas returned to free settlement, opening its doors to sawyers, farmers, fishermen and tourists. These days, the peninsula's cultural heritage is as renowned as its natural beauty. Outside the Park, numerous sites are scattered around the peninsula, including two of Australia's World Heritage convict sites – Port Arthur and the Coal Mines . Within the park, at Eaglehawk Neck , visit the Officer's Quarters beside the famous dogline. It was here that a line of fierce dogs was tethered across the narrow isthmus, guaranteed to change the minds of intending escapees. Getting there Show more/less Buy a map from TasMap Tasman National Park is located in the south-eastern corner of Tasmania. It's a 90-minute drive on sealed roads from Hobart via Sorell on the A3, and then the A9 (Arthur Highway) toward Port Arthur. The park straddles both the Tasman and Forestier peninsulas, however most of its accessible features are on the Tasman Peninsula. The Eaglehawk Neck Historic Site is accessible from the A9 at Eaglehawk Neck. ​After passing the Dogline on Eaglehawk Neck, take Blowhole Road (C338) then Tasmans Arch Road to Tasmans Arch and Devils Kitchen. The road is sealed and finishes at a car park with an all-access toilet. The location provides an option to commence the Tasman Trail and Waterfall Bay walk. The Tasman Trail and Waterfall Bay Walk are also accessible from Blowhole Road (338) by taking the mostly unsealed Waterfall Bay Road to its end at a car park with limited parking and no toilet. ​​​​​To reach Fortescue Bay from Eaglehawk Neck, continue along the A9 towards Port Arthur ​until you reach the junction with C344. Follow the C344 until you reach Fortescue Bay. This is a 12km drive along an unsealed road but is suitable for 2WD vehicles and mountain bikes. Beware of towing vehicles, delivery trucks and tour buses. Keep to the left of the road particularly on blind corners. Access to the south-western part of the park is also via the Arthur Highway (A9), then following Safety Cove Rd at Port Arthur township to access Remarkable Cave and walking tracks to Maingon Blowhole, Mount Brown and Crescent Bay. Further west, on the road to Nubeena, the access to the Cape Raoul Great Short Walk, Shipstern Bluff and Tunnel Bay leave the Arthur Highway at Highcroft Road, which turns into Stormlea Road. Where possible, please avoid driving in our reserves at night. You are sharing the roads with our native wildlife, so take it slow and watch out for animals on the road. Know before you go Show more/less ​​With the exception of designated areas in the Fortescue Bay campground, Tasman National Park is a Fuel Stove Only area and campfires are not permitted. To find out what fuel stoves are permitted see the Fuel Stove Only area ​page.​​ ​See Campfires and fire restrictions to find out what is permitted and where. Numerous accommodation and eating options are available on the Forestier and Tasman peninsulas. Fortescue Bay has limited food available at the campground office. More information ​Find out other essential information for visiting Tasmania's parks and reserves on our Know Before You Go web page . Safety message Show more/less Access friendly Show more/less There are four major attractions in this area and all the lookouts are within a 1 km drive of each other. Tasmans Arch and Devils Kitchen The car park has disabled car spaces with an adjacent all-access toilet facility. A wheelchair accessible circuit provides views of Tasmans Arch and Devils Kitchen. This circuit is flat with a sealed surface. A separate walking track accesses a coastal viewing platform. This track is not sealed, has a gravel surface and a gentle grade. The viewing platform is accessible via a ramp with a gentle grade. Wheelchair users may require assistance on this track. Tasman Blowhole This relatively wide loop track has some small inclines and does contain some stairs. Views of the blowhole are accessible from the gravel track, and the lookout provided has a level board surface. Fossil Bay This short gravel walking track has a steeper gradient with a step leading to the lookout at the top. These track features may make accessibility for wheelchair users more difficult and assistance may be required. There are accessible toilets at the Blowhole, although assistance may be required with the path leading from the carpark to the toilet block.
